newsitem.title: CHINA: HK vending machines find new coins indigestible.
newsitem.headline: HK vending machines find new coins indigestible.

text.p: Hit by collectors' fever over colonial-era coins featuring Britain's Queen Elizabeth, Hong Kong authorities rushed to mint 100 million new post-colonial coins to cope with a shortage of loose change.
The trouble began when thousands of vending machines across Hong Kong found the new coins indigestible and spat them out.
Payphone operators Hong Kong Telecom found phones were rejecting 10 percent of coins, and the Post office found that new 10 dollar coins were rejected, newspaper reports said on Friday.
This was despite the fact the new coins, made by the Royal Mint in Britain, had the same size, weight and metallic content as existing coins, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said.

"The coins are not 100 percent accepted by vending machines, there is a certain percentage of rejection. Situations like this happen all the time all over the world, not only in Hong Kong," spokesman Albert Chan told Reuters.
He said vending machines were so sensitive that even coins with slight scratches were sometimes rejected. "The range of five to 10 percent rejection is reasonable," he said.
Vending machine operators are seeking expert advice in Britain to solve the problem.

The coin shortage and the huge new issue of coins were sparked by a craze for hoarding the old colonial-era coins for their potential collector's value, following Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule on July 1. New issue coins bear a tropical flower emblem instead of the queen's head.
